questions.q: Induced currents do not occur only in coils and wires. According to the textbook, under which condition is an eddy current produced in a solid metal object?
options: Only when a steady magnetic field acts on a stationary metal object with no relative movement
When a magnetic field acts on part of a moving metal object, when a conductor is moving in an external magnetic field, or when a metal object is subjected to a changing magnetic field
Only when the metal object has been permanently magnetised beforehand
Only when a direct current is supplied to the metal through an attached wire
questions.explanation: The textbook lists three situations in which eddy currents occur: a magnetic field acting on part of a moving metal object, a conductor moving in an external magnetic field, or a metal object subjected to a changing magnetic field. In every case there is a changing magnetic flux through the bulk of the conductor, so an EMF is induced even though there is no wire or coil.

questions.q: Eddy currents resemble the eddies or swirls left in the water after a boat has gone by. Which statement correctly identifies the underlying principle the textbook gives for eddy currents?
options: Eddy currents are an application of Ohm's law and depend only on the resistance of the metal
Eddy currents are an application of Lenz's Law: the magnetic fields set up by the eddy currents oppose the changes in the magnetic field acting in the regions of the metal objects
Eddy currents reinforce the change in magnetic field that produced them, increasing the flux
Eddy currents are unrelated to electromagnetic induction and arise from static charge
questions.explanation: The textbook states eddy currents are an application of Lenz's Law: the magnetic fields set up by the eddy currents oppose the changes in the magnetic field acting in the regions of the metal objects. They can never reinforce the change, because that would create energy from nothing.

questions.q: A rectangular metal sheet moves relative to an external magnetic field, forming an eddy current loop. The side of the eddy current loop that is inside the magnetic field experiences a force. What does the textbook say about the direction of this force?
options: It is always in the same direction as the motion of the sheet, helping it along
It is always opposite to the direction of motion of the sheet, so it is harder to move the metal when the magnetic field is present than when the field is not present
It is zero, because the eddy current flows in a closed loop
It is perpendicular to the sheet, lifting it out of the field
questions.explanation: The textbook determines the direction of the force on the eddy current using the right-hand push rule, and it is always opposite to the direction of motion of the sheet. This means it is harder to move the metal through the region of magnetic field than to move it where no field is present.

questions.q: From memory, list the three situations the textbook describes in which eddy currents can occur in a metal object, given that induced currents do not occur only in coils and wires.
keyPoints: When a magnetic field acts on part of a metal object and there is relative movement between the magnetic field and the object.
When a conductor is moving in an external magnetic field.
When a metal object is subjected to a changing magnetic field.
questions.explanation: All three reduce to the same thing: a changing magnetic flux through the bulk of a conductor induces circulating eddy currents. If you recalled the moving-object, moving-conductor and changing-field cases, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: An induction cooker sets up a rapidly changing magnetic field that induces eddy currents in the metal of a saucepan placed on the cooktop. According to the textbook, why is this more efficient than a gas cooktop?
options: The ceramic top plate is heated first and then conducts heat into the saucepan, like a normal hotplate
The eddy currents cause the metal of the saucepan to heat up directly without the loss of thermal energy that occurs with gas cooking, giving an efficiency of about 80% against about 43% for gas
Gas cooktops cannot transfer any heat into the saucepan at all
The induction coil burns fuel more completely than a gas flame
questions.explanation: The changing magnetic field from the induction coil cuts through the metallic saucepan, causing eddy currents that heat the saucepan directly. Because the heat is produced in the saucepan itself rather than lost to the kitchen, induction cookers reach about 80% efficiency compared with about 43% for gas cookers.

questions.q: The changing magnetic field passing through the iron core of a transformer creates eddy currents. How does constructing the iron core from many thin layers reduce the heat losses due to these eddy currents?
options: The layers block the magnetic flux from passing through the core

By constructing the iron core from many layers of iron that are coated with an insulator, with cross-sections perpendicular to the direction of the magnetic flux, the size of the eddy currents is greatly reduced and the heating losses are reduced
The layers increase the conductivity of the core so current flows more freely
The layers turn the alternating flux into a steady direct flux
questions.explanation: A laminated iron core is built from many layers of iron, each coated with an insulator. The cross-sections of the thin layers are perpendicular to the direction of the magnetic flux, so the iron still carries the flux but the insulation breaks up the eddy-current paths, greatly reducing the size of the eddy currents and the heat losses.

questions.q: Besides laminating the core, the textbook describes another method for reducing eddy current losses in transformers using materials called ferrites. What property makes ferrites suitable?
options: They are good conductors of electricity but poor transmitters of magnetic flux
They are good transmitters of magnetic flux but poor conductors of electricity, so the magnitudes of eddy currents are significantly reduced
They completely block the magnetic flux so no current is needed
They generate larger eddy currents that cancel the original ones
questions.explanation: Ferrites are complex oxides of iron and other metals that are good transmitters of magnetic flux but poor conductors of electricity. Because eddy currents need a conducting path, their magnitudes are significantly reduced in a ferrite, cutting the heat losses.

questions.q: A roller-coaster car of mass 600 kg enters an electromagnetic braking section at 25 m s⁻¹ and is slowed to 5 m s⁻¹. How much kinetic energy is removed from the car?
questions.explanation: The kinetic energy removed is the initial minus the final kinetic energy. This 180 kJ is carried away by the induced eddy currents and dissipated as heat in the conducting rail by resistive heating: kinetic, to electrical, to heat.

questions.q: The same roller-coaster car loses 180 000 J of kinetic energy over a braking distance of 30 m. Using the work-energy theorem, find the average braking force.
working: Work done by the braking force equals the kinetic energy removed: \(W = \Delta E_k\)
\(F = 6\times 10^{3}\,\mathrm{N}\), directed opposite to the car's motion
questions.explanation: This 6000 N is an average. The real braking force is largest at 25 m s⁻¹ (where the flux changes fastest and the eddy current is biggest) and falls as the car slows, which is why an eddy-current brake alone cannot deliver the final stop.

questions.q: Explain how electromagnetic braking works, with reference to eddy currents and Lenz's law. (6 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: When a solid metal conductor, such as a train wheel, disc or fin, moves through an external magnetic field, the magnetic flux through the region of the metal inside the field changes. By Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction, this changing flux induces an EMF in the metal. Because the conductor is a solid bulk material rather than a wire, the induced EMF drives circulating closed loops of current within the body of the metal - these are eddy currents. By Lenz's law, the eddy currents flow in the direction that creates a magnetic field opposing the change in flux that produced them. As a result, the side of each eddy-current loop inside the external field is a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field, and experiences a force (F = BIL) that, by the right-hand push rule, always acts opposite to the direction of motion - a braking force. This opposing direction is required by conservation of energy: a force aiding the motion would create energy from nothing. The braking force does negative work, removing kinetic energy, which is transferred to the eddy currents and dissipated as heat by resistive heating. Because the EMF, current and force all grow with the rate of change of flux, the braking force increases with speed, making the braking smooth and contactless, but it falls to zero as the object stops, so it cannot by itself bring the object fully to rest.

criteria.descriptor: States that the moving conductor experiences a changing magnetic flux and, by Faraday's law, an EMF is induced.
Identifies eddy currents as circulating closed-loop currents in the bulk conductor.
Uses Lenz's law to establish the current direction opposes the change in flux.
Explains the resulting force (F = BIL) opposes the motion - a braking force.
Links the opposing direction to conservation of energy (no perpetual motion).
Traces the energy chain to heat and notes the force grows with speed (so cannot give the final stop).

questions.explanation: The marker rewards filling in every link: define eddy currents, produce them via Faraday, aim them via Lenz, derive the opposing force, justify it with conservation of energy, and trace the energy to heat. Swirl, drag, heat, fully expanded.
